an10.27:6.1: “Sir, in the morning we robed up and, taking our bowls and robes, entered Sāvatthī for alms.
an10.27:6.2: Then, sir, it occurred to us,
an10.27:6.3: ‘It’s too early to wander for alms in Sāvatthī.
an10.27:6.4: Why don’t we visit the monastery for the wanderers of other religions?’
an10.27:6.5: Then, sir, we went to the monastery for the wanderers of other religions and exchanged greetings with the wanderers there.
an10.27:6.6: When the greetings and polite conversation were over, we sat down to one side. Sir, the wanderers said to us:
an10.27:7.1: ‘Reverends, the ascetic Gotama teaches his disciples like this—
an10.27:7.2: Please, mendicants, directly know all things. Meditate having directly known all things.
an10.27:7.4: Please, reverends, directly know all things. Live having directly known all things.
an10.27:7.5: What, then, is the difference between the ascetic Gotama’s teaching and instruction and ours?’
an10.27:8.1: Sir, we neither approved nor rejected that statement of the wanderers of other religions.
an10.27:8.2: Neither approving nor rejecting, we rose from our seats and left, thinking,
an10.27:8.3: ‘We will learn the meaning of this statement from the Buddha himself.’”
an10.27:11.1: ‘Two things: question, summary recital, and answer.’ That’s what I said.
an10.27:11.2: But why did I say it?
an10.27:11.3: Becoming completely disillusioned, dispassionate, and freed regarding two things, seeing their limits and fully comprehending their meaning, a mendicant makes an end of suffering in this very life.
an10.27:11.6: Becoming completely disillusioned, dispassionate, and freed regarding these two things, seeing their limits and fully comprehending their meaning, a mendicant makes an end of suffering in this very life.
